source_work: The Flood Story (Eridu Genesis, ETCSL t.1.7.4)
note: Attests the Ancient Near Eastern deluge motif of a divinely warned righteous survivor (Ziusudra) preserving life in a vessel; contextual comparative parallel only.

source_work: Enki and Ninhursag (Dilmun Paradise Myth, ETCSL t.1.1.1)
note: Attests the Ancient Near Eastern paradisiacal garden motif of a pure, radiant land free of predation and sickness, irrigated by sweet springs.
Structural parallel between the rabbinic chain of oral transmission (shalshelet ha-qabbalah) from Sinai through generations of sages and the early Islamic isnad authentication tradition.
Shared Late Antique Near Eastern ethical maxim equating the preservation or destruction of a single human life with that of an entire world.

source_work: Procopius of Caesarea, History of the Wars (Wikisource)
note: Late Antique Byzantine eyewitness account of the Plague of Justinian (541-542 CE) contextualizing early Islamic plague-quarantine (ta'un) reports in Syria and the Levant.
Greco-Roman environmental and humoral health framework linking climate, seasonal winds, and water quality to bodily constitution, echoed in later Abbasid-era tibb literature.

source_work: Mu'allaqah of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma (Arabic Wikisource)
note: Pre-Islamic Arabian poetic ethos of peacemaking, blood-money settlement (diyah), and gnomic ethical maxims (hikmah) carried into early Islamic adab.

source_work: Mu'allaqah of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma (Arabic Wikisource)
locator: Mu'allaqah of Zuhayr, closing hikmah verses (datasets/sources/external/wikisource/muallaqah-zuhayr.txt)
note: Attests pre-Islamic Arabian proverbial wisdom on fate, generosity, and the futility of concealing character, circulating in Hijazi and Najdi oral folklore.
